A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching supplementary material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Deeprecon prediction and reconstruction analyses in Section 4 and original simulations in Section 6.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds quantitative naive-versus-sparse fMRI results and trial-noise estimates in Figure 9 and Appendices B.8–B.9.

M1.justification: The analyzed ridge regression, per-output correlation selection followed by ridge regression, and sparse teacher model are unchanged. The student–teacher terminology and expanded implementation descriptions do not introduce a different reconstruction method.

E1.justification: Both versions use Deeprecon natural images and artificial shapes and the same four synthetic generative conditions. The new comparisons and noise analysis use retained data and tasks, without adding a population or domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds a direct empirical feature-error comparison between correlation-filter-plus-ridge and naive ridge on Deeprecon in Figure 9B. v1 compares these designs theoretically, while its empirical ODC analyses compare naive predictions with the projection bound and show Shen et al.'s reconstructions as a visual reference. Earlier comparisons, including Ozcelik and VanRullen, remain.

E3.justification: The new comparison evaluates 50 natural test images using ridge penalties of 1000 for naive and 100 for sparse regression, with sample-dependent selected-voxel counts. v2 also adds a theoretical reference setting of sigma = 5; the original sigma = 0.1 simulations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 9 and Appendix B.8 add a noise diagnosis and an exploratory test of whether theory explains modest sparse-regression gains on real fMRI data. The original four simulation robustness conditions and ODC subsampling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.8 introduces an ANOVA-like estimation of stimulus variance and trial noise, reporting five training repetitions and 24 test repetitions. These are newly documented inputs to the analysis, not an asserted increase in experimental runs. Existing ODC error bars still show standard deviation across images.

E6.justification: v2 adds empirical error curves for 150, 300, 600 and 1200 training images, showing a modest sparse-regression advantage, alongside high-noise theoretical curves. Appendix B.8 newly reports noise-to-signal estimates of about 5.7 and 5.2 for training and test data. Existing ODC and simulation results are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B.8 adds a random-effects model, expected mean-square relations and variance-component estimators. The central output-subspace argument, projection bound, sparse-regression risk expression and selection-rate/hit-rate derivation remain mathematically unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion narrow the emphasis from demonstrating accurate sparse prediction at small data scales to specifying when it is achievable within the student–teacher framework. Analytic ODC diagnosis also becomes an explicit main contribution, while the central ODC claim is retained.

C2.justification: v1 already discusses high noise and uncertain real-world sparsity. v2 connects modest empirical gains to measured noise, explicitly disclaims an immediate recipe for large improvements, and limits the theory–data comparison to relative errors because their absolute scales differ. It also expands discussion of accurate image recovery despite latent-feature perturbations.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: subject and ROI, feature standardization, category-balanced subsampling, ridge penalties, DIP optimization settings, simulation regularization and sparse voxel counts are documented in Appendices B.3, B.7 and B.9. It also adds a GitHub code hyperlink. Much of this newly specifies existing experiments rather than establishing changed execution.

R1.justification: v2 adds Onoo et al. (2025) and Lee et al. (2025) to support discussion of generator recovery under latent perturbations, and removes Allen et al. (2022) and Hebart et al. (2023). The principal positioning relative to prior ODC and sparse-regression research remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial portions of Sections 5–7 are rewritten, with revised terminology and contribution framing. Filter details move to Appendix B.5, the conclusion is integrated into the discussion, and the appendices are reorganized. The title and author information change, and v1's AI-use declaration is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts different typography, margins and title/author formatting. It combines v1 Figures 7–8 into Figure 7 and Figures 9–10 into Figure 8, adds Figure 9, and relocates the supplementary figures. Existing plots and reconstruction examples are retained within this substantial presentation revision.

improvement.justification: Figure 9 and Appendix B.8 give empirical support to v1's largely qualitative explanation of modest real-data gains, while expanded settings and the code link improve reproducibility information. Claims are better qualified. The improvement is limited because the new theory–data connection remains exploratory, with unknown sparsity and different error scales, while the central theory and earlier results are unchanged.
